newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya says tea production to drop in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kenya says tea production to drop in 1997.

text.p: Capricious weather will cut production of tea, Kenya's leading commodity export, in 1997 from 1996 but farmers hope better prices will compensate for the loss.
"1997 started off very badly with all districts having to cope with severe drought conditions," Musa Sang, chairman of the farmers' group Kenya Tea Growers Association (KTGA), told Reuters.
"First came the hailstorms suffered by Kericho in January, and to some lesser degree Sotik district, and then the rains disappeared completely (in February and March)," he said.
He said KTGA members had suspended or cut drastically capital spending and in March tea estates worked an average of only three days per week.
"We will only hope that the current improved tea auction prices in Mombassa and other auction centres will be maintained in order to compensate for the shortfall in the crop," he said.
Although rains have returned to key tea growing areas, Sang suggested that enough damage had already been done to reduce Kenya's crop, but he was not drawn into providing figures.

Kenya's tea production rose to 257 million kg in 1996 compared with 244 million kg in 1995. Of that, 106 million kg or 41.24 percent was produced by KTGA members, who hold 26.48 percent of the 110,000 hectares of planted tea in Kenya.

Kenya's tea exports reached a record 244 million kg in 1996 for 21.6 billion shillings ($393.4 million) in hard currency. That was higher than Sri Lanka's 243.5 million kg and made Kenya the world's leading exporter of black teas.

Sang said ideal growing conditions were responsible for the 1996 record crop but demand was not enough to support prices at competitive levels. He said prices fell steadily throughout the year and in the second half many farmers sold at below the cost of production.

"If tea producers are to restore their competitive position in the tea world to its 1992 level in hard currency costs, we need to see an exchange rate of at least 60 shillings or even 65 per dollar," Sang said.
Sang said the KTGA was concerned Kenya continued to rely on three main markets.

Britain was the leading buyer of Kenyan tea in 1996 with 77 million kg followed by Pakistan with 55.5 million kg and then Egypt. The three accounted for 74 percent of Kenya's total tea exports in 1996.
Sang said roads were relatively well maintained after the government gave the responsibility of collecting farm levies for road repair to grower committees instead of local authorities.
He said KTGA members still had power shortages, which the Kenya Power & Lighting Co (KP&LC) partly blames on drought. Power has been rationed in Kenya for almost a year.
"Members are being disconnected up to eight hours each day, leaving them no alternative but to buy standby generators which are very costly," Sang said.
Sang said a major KTGA headache was slow refunding of Value Added Tax, offered by the government as in incentive. Sang said some 215 million shillings was held by government in refunds.
He said farmers were concerned about heavy taxation on tea. He listed at least six taxes and called for rationalisation that would result in one amalgamated tax.
